about: Every finding scripts/parity.mjs makes must match a rule here, or the script fails.
Three verdicts now: OURS, PORT, DONE.
SHAPE is gone. It held the pieces where upstream has the same capability by another
structure — the file store, the folder view, the HTTP layer — on the grounds that
nxzai#373 placed them outside its plan. The goal is `main` upstream equal to
`integration`, not upstream merely able to do everything `integration` does, and
those are not the same statement. So they are PORT, in batches P3-37 to P3-40,
each saying in its note that it is offered rather than owed: the maintainer scoped
them out once and may do so again.
OURS is now only what cannot go: our release workflows and packaging, the demo,
our planning documents and release notes, our own tooling, the quick-actions menu
upstream closed in nxzai#333, and the files upstream has that we do not.
Batches are numbered P3-nn, phase 3, in delivery order. The thirty-three of
nxzai#373 were phase 2. P3-01 to P3-04 are sent and waiting on the maintainer.
The first matching rule wins, so the specific ones come first. `match` is a
regular expression unless `exact` is true. There is deliberately no catch-all:
anything new is unclassified, and unclassified is a failure.

rules.note: the application asking a question in its own voice — P3-58 when it goes. `window.confirm`, `window.prompt` and `alert` were still answering for twenty-three questions and messages, and what they draw is the browser's box in the browser's chrome, headed by the server's address and port, over a question about somebody's file. `useAsk` keeps the one thing they gave for free — a call that waits for the answer — and everything from a tab's guard to the cross on the tab waits with it. Goes as one piece: the dialog, the composable, and the screens that stopped asking the browser.

the answer to the question before a token is revoked, which `window.confirm` used to be an expression in an `if`: a dialog answers with a promise, so the answer is read into something before it is tested.

two screens that had been sent and were in step again, changed by the dialog batch and so drifted again: both asked the browser for a name and one asked it to confirm a revocation. comparing two or three files side by side, as WinMerge does — P3-60 when it goes. `utils/testing/routerAddress.js` travels with it: a comparison's address is a key that several screens build and one screen reads back, and every suite that touches one mocks the router away, so the stand-in that spells an address the way the router spells it is shared rather than written out three times. `textDiff.js` is the alignment, written here rather than taken from a library because the answer has to be aligned and not merely listed: a patch says what changed, a comparison has to put line 40 of one file beside the line it corresponds to in the other, with a gap where there is nothing to put. `CompareView.vue` is the screen that walks the differences and takes one side over the other; `config/compare.js` decides what can be compared — whatever the text editor opens, plus whatever `COMPARE_FILE_EXTENSIONS` adds, because what counts as text is a local question. `compareSessions.js` is what a tab is in the middle of comparing — the files, their lines as they now stand, the difference the reader was on. Declared before the rule that owns the preview plugins, which was written when every file under them had already been sent and cannot speak for files that did not exist. `SettingsTabs.vue` is where an administrator says how many tabs a row may hold, since the strip never scrolls and the row has to stop somewhere. A terminal is a place now: what a terminal *is* came out of the drawer that showed it (`TerminalSurface.vue`) so that a page at an address of its own can show one too, and there can be as many shells as there are tabs. `TerminalHost.vue` and `stores/terminal.js` are the other half of the same move: a terminal belongs to the tab it was opened from, so the store keeps one session per tab and the host draws every one of them and outlives every page — a page is unmounted the moment another tab comes forward, and an unmounted terminal is a killed shell. `NavButtons.vue` is the pair of buttons that walk a tab’s own trail, which is the same batch’s answer to a window whose history belonged to nobody in particular. `tabWarmup.js` is the same batch getting a tab ready before the reader reaches it — a tab opened behind was an address and nothing else, so a folder was listed, a viewer built and a document server reached only once it was brought forward. It fills the places that already outlive a page, and `documentRoute.js` gained the one thing it needed: an address read back as the entry it names, which the document page works out from its own route parameters and anything preparing a tab it is not on cannot. `tabLoading.js` is which tabs are still working, so the strip can say so where their icon goes — a tab got ready in the background does its work while the reader is looking at something else, and without a word from it there is nothing to tell "not there yet" from "there, and empty". `SpinnerIcon.vue` exists because the one this fork already had cannot be told a size: its box comes from a font-size in a global stylesheet and the scale that makes it look smaller is a transform, so in a row of tabs it was twice the height of the row and pushed the page down. `tabGuards.js` is what a tab has to say before it is closed: closing is the one gesture that destroys what a tab was holding, and the tabs store cannot judge it because it holds addresses and not work — so a screen with something to lose leaves a question for its own tab, and a tab nobody asked about closes exactly as it always has

tabs, lot 1: a folder per tab, the kinds a tab can hold, the strip, and the switch that offers any of it — P3-59 when it goes, and where an entry opens, which three of them ask. `utils/tabDrag.js` travels with the strip: a tab being dragged says so under a name of its own, rather than as text that happens to look like an id, and a drop target has to decide during `dragover` — when a browser refuses to hand the data over. `composables/paneBoxes.js` travels with the terminal host, which is the first thing that has to know where its tab's box is: what draws a shell lives above every layout so that it survives its tab going behind another, and it therefore cannot be positioned by nesting. One pane and the answer is the content area, which is what it assumed; said out loud here, and the one place a second pane later has to change

two tabs at once, side by side, with one sidebar — the next batch after the comparison. What belongs to a place is the pane's own and what belongs to a person stays one to the window, which is the line `files/folderTab.js` already drew: `paneTab.js` is how a screen on the far side of it asks which side it is on, `TabPane.vue` is a pane. The rest is the panes' own state in the store, the two of them drawn by the layout, the entry in the strip's menu, the folder view and the breadcrumb reading their pane instead of the tab in front, and the drag that now reads the folder the files arrived in. A pair is a grouping of two *tabs* rather than a split of the window, so there can be as many as there are tabs: `paneBoxes.js` measures where each pane is, for the two things drawn outside the page that have to sit on it anyway — a document in its viewer and a shell. Both are told which panes are on screen instead of which tab is in front, and both take their box from there rather than from the window. The window is the window: `WindowSidebar.vue` and `WindowBar.vue` are what the browser layout used to hold, drawn once above every layout so that a pane can hold anything — a document and a shell are outside that layout on purpose, and the editor and a comparison are in another. `composables/sidebar.js` is a module-level singleton because the toolbar above a pane has to open the same sidebar the window draws
